item.title: The 'Astra can read and write weights to improve Qwen' post is misleading
item.description:
Source: honnibal.dev

Top Comment:

I work in this field (mech interp research) and I agree, the original post is definitely misleading. Some overselling in research is normal but it's a bit much.

First, the key result has nothing to do with making Qwen better at math, it just reduces reasoning loops.

Reasoning loops are a simple problem: the model generates the </think> token (which closes reasoning) with too low probability. You can fix this with simple steering approaches where you add a vector to different components of the LLM (https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.22048, https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.18167, etc). The method Astra used for identifying the vector is the standard procedure humans use (contrastive analysis). Such steering vector creation is basically the standard "intro-level interp project" for human researchers.

If you can code and understand LLM internals, you can do this yourself in 4-8 hours. The SWE equivalent would be doing binary patching with a debugger. Cool that frontier models can do this, but not unexpected since humans can do it without issue.

item.title: Could a modern chess engine on a Pentium have defeated Kasparov in 1996?
item.description:
Source: nicholas.carlini.com

Top Comment:

The main point the post is trying to make is accurate, modern chess engines are stronger mostly due to improved eval, search, etc and not hardware; but the idea that Kasparov would lose to one on 90s hardware is not as clearly true as one might think. Modern engine eval functions and search algos make very different depth tradeoffs and when given not enough compute they have glaring weaknesses that Kasparov and his team would likely have exploited.

It was trivial for me an expert-ish player (1950 USCF 2300+ bullet) to find a line to beat it. https://nicholas.carlini.com/writing/2026/algorithmic-improv...

Also 3000 engine elo is not really a good direct comparison, engine elos are kinda meaningless when comparing human to engines, they are meant to compare engines to engines.

A lot of the knowledge tricks that modern engines do require depth or other things that didn't work on older hardware, deep blue was engineered to brute force a lot of things because brute force in the 90s worked better. Historically all sorts of things were tried for chess engines abandoned and tried again. Chess engine dev (and AI in general) is very cyclical; old ideas get returned to and retried as the hardware changes and evolves. Devs from past eras were smarter and more knowledgeable than we give them credit for. Heck, some of the very first engines for checkers and chess were neural nets (of a sort).

item.title: Fujifilm to boost tape production 5x as AI fuels archiving demand
item.description:
Source: arstechnica.com

Top Comment:

Anyone that's never had the (dis)pleasure of working with tapes, there's some gotchas to know about before archiving and forgetting about it.

When you create an archive, do not skip the step of reading it back. I'm not talking about just having the system confirm it is readable. I mean actually restoring the data from the tape. I've had tapes fail to retrieve data off of the tape even though the writing app confirmed it was readable.

Drives can have issues reading data written by another drive. Drives can have issues reading a tape it wrote itself.

Why write one when you can write two at twice the time/cost? In all of my experience with tape, I've never written just one tape. In the early days of DVDs, the images were written to LTO to send to have the discs pressed. Two were always sent on the chance one wasn't readable and schedules were so tight that the loss of a couple of days to send a new tape would wreck delivery dates. Another facility wrote three tapes: one kept on site, one sent to IronMountain, one sent to the client directly. Plenty of occasions saw the local copy unreadable and the IronMountain copy was retrieved. These were managed by large robotic tape libraries so each tape was written in a different drive at the same time so it was 3x cost while only 1x time.

Use the drive cleaning cassette as recommended. Your dirty heads can cause the data to not be written/read correctly depending on which head is dirty. If you're having issues reading, clean the heads before giving up on the tape. If you're having issues reading a tape just written, do not think someone else will be able to read it.

Ensure whoever might be using a tape you've written understands what was used to write the tape. Not all archivers are compatible. If you use the tar command to write to tape, people using a GUI app won't be able to read it.

item.title: Resisting Cognitive Surrender
item.description:
Source: knlb.dev

Top Comment:

I think there's a paradox. Is it only "cognitive surrender" if you already know how to code? Not knowing all the details seems more like the default human condition, in the sense that most people don't know exactly where their water comes from or where their waste goes exactly. "Water comes from the tap, food comes from the store".

Most of the non-technical people I see using LLMs to create software are not engaging in "cognitive surrender" as far as I can tell.

They didn't read the code before and they don't now. However, asking questions and improving understanding of the system and architecture is actually faster and easier for them now than it used to be.

They're evaluating what they can see, i.e, judging results. They build things for their own use. They test them, iterate on them to meet their needs and try to achieve their vision. This is roughly the same process they followed when they used to outsource to an agency except the loop is much tighter.

It seems to work well, mainly hurts when the problems are invisible, so security, backups, breaking migrations, perf, maintenance over time (language / runtime updates, dep updates, server updates etc). All the stuff that hurts if you have never been responsible for the uptime of something before. Not knowing that software is never "done". But junior devs trip on those exact same things.

I agree with the tail of the article; tooling and processes that make that stuff more visible would close a lot of the gaps.

item.title: Launch HN: Momentic (YC W24) – Agents that catch bugs by using your app
item.description:
Source: momentic.ai

Hey HN, we’re Wei-Wei and Jeff. We’re building Momentic, QA agents that autonomously plan, explore, and bug-bash controls and user flows in your web, iOS, Android, and (soon) desktop apps to catch bugs.

Here’s a demo: https://youtu.be/BFsM-Se1Fh8

We’re both software engineers that spent our careers on dev tooling and infra across companies like Robinhood, Retool, WeWork, and Qualtrics. Testing was always a pain in the ass (esp Playwright and Selenium), so we built agents to do it for us.

Modern day software has a ton of bugs and the change failure rate is only growing faster as coding agent adoption scales. LLMs are really good at generating code, but reinforce their own assumptions, write a ton of useless tests, and are bad at visual understanding. On DeepSWE v1.1, Sonnet 5.5 hit 66.2% pass rate when banned from writing tests, versus 65.3% when allowed.

OSS end-to-end testing frameworks like Playwright, Selenium, or Maestro force you to hardcode implementation details like XPath, text, or aria-* attributes in your tests. Even with agents, these take a nontrivial amount of time and tokens to build and maintain.

In 2023, we saw Nat Friedman drive a browser with GPT-3 via natbot. We were inspired to use this technology to automate the most painful and tedious parts of software engineering: testing. We started with using LLMs to generate and maintain Playwright, but quickly realized that those primitives were fundamentally misaligned with the agentic SDLC. We think the future of QA is agents testing themselves, not writing scripts.

Mo is a custom agent harness for catching bugs that builds on the past 3 years of Momentic and millions of test traces from complex, real-world applications. Mo is built for recall: it finds the most real bugs, though Codex is a bit more precise at 86% vs 84%. The tradeoff is cost: Mo costs $2.67 per bug vs $0.80 for Codex, less than Claude Code and Devin.

- Self-organizing agent graph. Mo builds a directed acyclic graph (DAG) as it explores. Large product areas automatically fork into parallel sub-agents, each with their own browser or device for concurrent execution.

- Specialized agents for domain specific tasks. Planner agents reason over screenshots and video while dedicated locator agents inspect page structure to resolve plain-English interaction targets. Others include image analysis, video understanding, audio generation, and more.

- Parallel agents coordinate through cooperative resource leases. Agents can announce that they’re “using” or “modifying” overlapping resources or fixtures. Multiple “using” claims can coexist, but only a single “modifying” claim can be active on any particular one.

- Scaled infrastructure. Mo ships with a tunnel that lets users expose private sites and local apps to our hosted agents and infra. A single bug bash can spin up 100s of concurrent browsers and devices.

We benchmarked Mo against coding agents on 4 popular open-source apps: Gitea (58.8k stars), Metabase, Twenty (YC), and Saleor, with 1,396 human-labeled bugs. Each agent got the same brief, a fresh E2B sandbox, and no access to source code. Codex and Claude Code used hosted Browserbase browsers, while Devin used its built-in browser. For evaluators, we implemented LLM as a judge (GPT-6.1 Sol) with a human reviewer.

Results from a time-boxed 60-minute run:

- Mo: 269 bugs, 19.3% recall, 84% precision, $2.67 per bug

- Codex (GPT-6.1 Sol + Playwright MCP): 86 bugs, 6.2% recall, 86% precision, $0.80 per bug

- Claude Code (Opus 5.5 + Playwright MCP): 59 bugs, 4.2% recall, 80% precision, $4.09 per bug

- Devin: 27 bugs, 1.9% recall, 84% precision, $3.89 per bug

Mo finds more bugs the more time it has. From 30 to 60 minutes, it went from 177 to 269 bugs (+52%), while Codex gained only 16%.

Results: https://momentic.ai/qa-bench

Write-up: https://momentic.ai/blog/qa-bench

Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/momentic/qa-bench

Harness: https://github.com/momentic-ai/qa-bench

We just shipped PR testing for Vercel and Cloudflare deploy previews and we’re giving every new signup $250 in Mo spend. Paid plans have higher infra capacity and included usage along with options to top up.

We’d love for you to try it out and give us feedback. Feel free to comment here, we’ll be around all day!
